articles.title: The creator of Claude Code's Claude setup
articles.summary: Boris Cherny @bcherny I'm Boris and I created Claude Code. Lots of people have asked how I use Claude Code, so I wanted to show off my setup a bit. Claude Code works great out of the box, so I personally don't customize it much. There is no one correct way to use Claude Code: we intentionally build it in a way that you can use it, customize it, and hack it however you like.

articles.title: Claude Code On-the-Go
articles.summary:
I run six Claude Code agents in parallel from my phone. The loop is: kick off a task, pocket the phone, get notified when Claude needs input. Git worktrees let me run multiple features simultaneously:
Each worktree gets its own tmux window with a Claude agent. The setup took one Claude Code session to build—gave it my Vultr API key and access to gh , asked for a secure dev VM.

articles.summary: I’ve been using Claude Code more and more recently. At some point I realized that rather than do something else until it finishes, I would constantly check on it to see if it was asking for yet another permission, which felt like it was missing the point of having an agent do stuff. So I wanted to use Claude Code with the --dangerously-skip-permissions flag. articles.title: Claude Chill: Fix Claude Code's flickering in terminal
articles.summary:
A PTY proxy that tames Claude Code's massive terminal updates using VT-based rendering. Claude Code uses synchronized output to update the terminal atomically. The problem: Claude Code sends entire screen redraws in these sync blocks - often thousands of lines. This causes lag, flicker, or jitters in the terminal, making for a poor user experience.
claude-chill sits between your terminal and Claude Code:
Or, if you've cloned the repository locally:
Press Ctrl+6 (or your configured key) to enter lookback mode:

articles.title: I'm 60 years old. Claude Code killed a passion
articles.story_text:
I stumble upon a post from shannoncc called "I'm 60 years old. Claude Code has re-ignited a passion", and it made me think. I am also (almost) 60, but AI just killed the passion. I remember all the pre-AI days, where I was enjoying coding during the day, the evening, the weekends and the vacations. This is no more, while others have their "passion re-ignited".

I would argue it depends on what you enjoy: the journey or the destination. I have always enjoyed the journey,
articles.summary: I have coworkers who get itchy when they don't see their work on production, and super defensive in code review but I've never really cared. If it takes a week to get through code review, what do I care, I'm already off to the next puzzle. Being forced to use Claude at work, it really just took away everything that was enjoyable. Agentic coding is just faster at the 20% part, and I can always sit down and code the really hard stuff if I want to or feel I need to if the LLM gets stuck.

articles.title: Natural Language Autoencoders: Turning Claude's Thoughts into Text
articles.summary: When you talk to an AI model like Claude, you talk to it in words. These numbers in the middle are called activations— and like neural activity in the human brain, they encode Claude’s thoughts. We can’t easily decode them to read Claude’s thoughts. Over the past few years, we’ve developed a range of tools (like sparse autoencoders and attribution graphs ) for better understanding activations.

articles.title: Why Ctrl+V won't paste images in Claude Code on WSL, with a fix
articles.summary: tl;dr Use Claude Code in WSL inside Windows Terminal? Copying an image in Windows and pressing Ctrl+V in Claude Code doesn't work. Three things break: (1) WSL only hands Windows images to the Linux side in an old BMP format Claude Code can't read; (2) WSL also keeps quietly overwriting your fixes a moment later; (3) Windows Terminal grabs Ctrl+V before Claude Code can see it. articles.summary: Today we're introducing dynamic workflows in Claude Code, helping Claude take on the most challenging tasks end-to-end.
